criterion_notes.c1: No. The paper examines upstream watershed and aquifer recharge area protection (specifically land-use encroachment, deforestation, and siltation in the Guacerique watershed and Los Laureles reservoir supplying Tegucigalpa), not household or community water or sanitation service access. Consumer water coverage and flat-fee tariffs are mentioned only briefly as policy background to contrast service-delivery priorities against neglected source-water stewardship (Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access).
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper broadly discusses legal, institutional, and governance issues—including unapplied watershed protection laws (the 1973 Protected Forestry Zone statute and 1981 restricted-development declaration), inter-agency fragmentation across SANAA, COHDEFOR, and environmental ministries, IMF-linked budget cuts to SANAA's watershed management unit, and water-sector privatization pressures—so a broad literal reading not tied to service access could view governance factors as present, though governing catchment land use rather than consumer access (plain_criterion2_decision remains exclude because c1, c3, c4, and c5 all fail). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is 'no' because none of these forestry/zoning statutes or watershed budget decisions are rule-type mechanisms directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation rules, connection/tariff rules, or service enforcement).
criterion_notes.c3: No. The article is a narrative policy commentary and descriptive overview drawing on secondary reports (e.g., SANAA/public ministry technical reports and UNDP statistics) with no empirical research methodology, no primary data collection, no analytical design, and no systematic empirical synthesis.
criterion_notes.c4: No. Reported outcomes concern upstream land-use conversion, reservoir sedimentation and carryover storage loss, raw water turbidity/algal blooms/fecal coliform counts, and chemical water-treatment costs, rather than household or community water or sanitation access, connection, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: No. As a non-empirical policy essay on watershed protection, there is no identifiable empirical study design, no sampled population or unit of analysis for service access, and no measured service-access exposure-outcome relationship.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is written in English.

exposure: Upstream urban land-use encroachment, non-enforcement of watershed forestry and zoning protections, fragmented institutional responsibilities, and budget cuts to SANAA's watershed management unit
outcome: Watershed degradation, reservoir siltation and carryover storage loss, raw water turbidity and pathogen contamination, and increased raw water treatment costs
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic; see Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). The paper focuses on upstream watershed and source-water protection in the Guacerique catchment and Los Laureles reservoir supplying Tegucigalpa, Honduras—specifically land-use encroachment, non-enforcement of forestry/zoning laws, reservoir siltation, raw water contamination, and cuts to SANAA's watershed management budget—explicitly contrasting neglected watershed protection with downstream consumer coverage expansion. In addition, it is a non-empirical narrative policy overview relying on secondary reports with no primary data or identifiable empirical study design (failing c1, c2 under the narrow rule-type reading, c3, c4, and c5).
